nameStory: The name 'unimaculatus' means 'one spot' in Latin, likely referring to a single distinctive marking on this spider's body. As a member of the stealthy ground spiders, it earned its family name from their secretive hunting behavior - they prowl silently across the ground at night rather than building webs to catch prey.
description: This is a small, dark ground spider that hunts by prowling rather than web-building. Like other stealthy ground spiders, it has a compact, somewhat flattened body that's typically dark brown to blackish in color. Adults reach only about 3-6mm in body length, making them quite small and easy to overlook as they scurry across soil and leaf litter.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small spider, only 3-6mm in body length - about the size of a pencil eraser or smaller

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, somewhat flattened body that feels firm if gently touched, with relatively long legs for its body size

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Dark brown to blackish coloration with a single distinctive pale spot or marking on the abdomen (the 'one spot' of its scientific name)

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Active hunter that runs quickly across the ground at night; during day hides under stones or in leaf litter where it feels cool and slightly damp

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Does not build a capture web, but may create small silk retreats under rocks that feel like thin, papery tubes

habitat: Look for this secretive spider in dry to moderately moist habitats including forest floors, fields, and gardens throughout New England's lower elevations. They prefer areas with loose soil, leaf litter, or scattered rocks where they can easily hide during daylight hours. Often found under stones, logs, or in the spaces between fallen leaves where the ground stays cool and slightly humid.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter shelters under rocks and deep leaf litter to hunt small insects.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly encountered hunting at night across open ground and forest floors.
seasonality.fall: Mating season when you might spot pairs together; adults prepare overwintering retreats in protected locations.
seasonality.winter: Inactive, hiding deep in rock crevices, under logs, or in thick leaf litter where they remain dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Despite being incredibly rare in New England with only one recorded observation, this tiny spider is an accomplished night hunter that can run down prey many times larger than itself, including small beetles and even other spiders!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small, dark ground spiders in the same family, but the single pale spot on the abdomen is the key distinguishing feature - other similar species either lack spots entirely or have multiple markings rather than just one.
contextualKnowledge: This species is extraordinarily rare in New England with only a single confirmed observation, making it one of our region's least-known spiders. It's possible that it's more common than records suggest but simply overlooked due to its tiny size and secretive nighttime habits.
compareHints: Among its Sergiolus relatives, this species is distinguished by having just one pale spot rather than the multiple spots or complex patterns seen in the Variegated Ground Spider or Common Patterned Ant-mimic Ground Spider. While other Sergiolus species may have elaborate markings or even mimic ants in their appearance, S. unimaculatus keeps it simple with its single diagnostic spot.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Sergiolus relatives, the Variegated Ground Spider is distinguished by its particularly mottled, bark-like camouflage pattern.
